tests.description: Commands we decline to run even with approval, matched by command word and by the last part of a path. Only the destructive spellings of git subcommands are refused, and only in the first argument position. A `--` after checkout or restore names paths to discard, so it is refused, and `--` after another git subcommand is not.

What tarsec 0.5.7 lets through. `--` is a flag no table lists, so ls, echo, and cd with one are broad. A program with no rule takes `--` as an argument, so `pnpm test -- --watch` asks std::exec. A `~` or `^` inside a word is plain text: a redirect to `a~b` writes a file of that name. A `~` after `=` is still not parsed.

Each recognized command contributes its own effects. An unrecognized command, an unknown flag, a non-literal command word and a leading assignment are all unrecognized. In a sequence, echo contributes nothing whatever its arguments, because bash runs it.

A redirect writes a file whatever the verb is, so it contributes std::write independently. A variable target, an input redirect on echo, a descriptor other than 2, or two output redirects is unrecognized.

A redirect of standard output or standard error to /dev/null writes no file, so it adds no effect. 2>file asks std::write for that file, with the same overwrite and append modes as >file, and descriptor 1 means the same as no descriptor. &>/dev/null is still broad. Any other descriptor, a second output file, or a variable target stays broad. The rebuilt text keeps the redirect.

The whole string gets one plan: refused if any command anywhere is refused, one std::bash if any command is unrecognized, otherwise the union of narrow effects. Chains are walked, so `true && dd if=a of=b` is refused rather than approvable.
A narrow plan runs the tree it classified (whitespace normalized, and a git command written by safeBash with the git tools' fixed flags); a broad plan runs the caller's text verbatim.

A single fully-literal echo computes its own output and never touches a shell. An expansion, a sequence, a flag other than -n, a flag after the first word, or a quoted word that starts with a dash sends it to bash, because bash reads the quoted dash as the option too.

A single literal redirected echo computes its content and writes it, with no shell. The `>` and `>>` rows differ only in mode, which is the difference between overwriting and appending. A variable TARGET is unrecognized entirely; a variable in the ARGUMENTS is still recognized and goes to bash raising std::write with no content — approval of the destination, not the bytes. Non-write plans report only the fields their Execution variant carries.
Payload values, not just effect names. A staged diff and an unstaged diff raise the same effect name, so only the payload distinguishes them.
The std::write interrupt carries the bytes, so a policy that inspects what is being written still can.
A literal echo returns its text with no interrupt and no shell.
The narrow question REPLACES the broad one. Approving std::git::status runs the command; a second std::bash prompt would fail the run on an unmatched interrupt.

tests.description: Each git read asks the effect its git tool raises, with the payload filled from the command's own words. A flag that only changes how the result is shown, or shows less, keeps the rule.

Words before a `--` are refs and words after it are paths, whether or not they exist. With no `--`, a word that names a file or folder is a path and any other word is a ref. A word after `--` that looks like a flag has no rule.
Each git write asks the effect its git tool raises. `commit -a` asks for the staging as well. `checkout -b` asks std::git::switch with create.

Every git spelling with no rule asks std::bash: a flag that shows more or does something else, a second message, a bare `git add`, an unquoted `~`, a start point, a forced form, a glob, a path where the effect has no field for one, a leading flag or assignment, and a subcommand with no effect.
A chain of recognized git commands is narrow and asks each effect in order. A pipe into a filter needs only the git question. One command with no rule makes the whole string broad.
`git restore --staged` takes files out of the index and has a rule, with or without a `--`. Any other restore discards work and is refused.
`git checkout` with a second word beside the ref overwrites that file, so it is refused, whatever tag the parser gave the word. `-b` and `-B` take a start point and are not refused.

safeBash writes the git command it runs: the git tools' fixed flags, the checked flags, and a `--` between refs and paths. A diff runs behind a check that git sees a work tree. Redirects are kept and asked about. Every spelling of a flag runs as the built one, and a value is always quoted.
